newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil union says pay victory just a beginning.
newsitem.headline: Brazil union says pay victory just a beginning.

text.p: A Brazilian trade union representing federal civil servants celebrated Thursday a controversial pay claim victory by pledging to win similar cases for up to a million workers and pensioners.

"We are demanding that the 28.9 percent (pay raise) be extended to everyone and we are asking workers to bring us their pay slips so we can begin new cases," said Luiz Bicalho, general secretary of the Federal Workers Union (Sindisep).
The Supreme Federal Tribunal, Brazil's highest court, ruled Wednesday that 11 federal civil servants were entitled to a 28.9 percent pay rise awarded to the armed forces in 1993.
The government fears the decision may set a precedent for about one million federal workers and pensioners seeking similar increases and upset its drive to curb public spending.
About 200,000 federal workers have already filed suits in courts across the country to demand identical pay raises and unions are encouraging others to begin legal action.
In the bustling corridors of Sindsep's headquarters in Brasilia, pensioners waited in line to fill out forms that will lead to court cases.

Seated beneath a painting of angry-looking 19th century miners on the march for social justice, Bichalho dismissed the government's claims that Wednesday's ruling might damage its Real Plan to cut inflation and sort out public finances.
"The Real Plan is terrible for Brazil. It has caused nothing but unemployment, misery and hunger. If it goes under, we won't be crying," he said.
As well as the 28.9 percent, federal worker unions were seeking to negotiate pay raises of 64 percent to make up for what it says are losses to inflation in 1995 and 1996.
They also want the government to scrap its reforms of the civil service and pensions system, which seek to cut public sector jobs and benefits to reduce costs.

Despite Wednesday's victory, Bicalho admitted the unions faced a long struggle ahead, principally because the government would probably seek to bog down progress on the pay claims in Brazil's notoriously slow justice system.
The union leader said the government had another small advantage in the form of a law allowing it to delay making backdated payments.

That meant the 11 victorious civil servants must wait until the year 2000 for salary increases backdated to 1993 although new suits being drawn up by union lawyers would entitle workers to backdated pay in 1998 if their cases are settled this year.
Bicalho, like government officials, said he had no idea how much a federal government-wide pay increase of 28.9 percent would actually cost.
Newspapers have estimated backdated payments could go as high as $20 billion with another $7.0 billion needed to cover the increase this year.
